account:
Before the window, Project Lanternleaf was framed as a two-imprint pilot, with Contributor 01 assigned the exception rules and prototype while Contributor 07 owned the source export. The system produced advisory flags only, did not place payment holds, and left decisions with Publishing Operations.

Contributor 01 requested currency and reversal-reference fields, designed a four-part exception taxonomy with plain-language reasons, and implemented four advisory rules, fixture tests, configurable outlier thresholds and a test queue exposing filters and source fields. Thresholds were provisional; reversal matching fell back to amount-and-date heuristics when references were absent, and the prototype did not update payment status.

After Contributor 06 identified title-level duplicate false alarms and Contributor 09 found cross-currency reversal pairing, Contributor 01 revised the duplicate key, added an insufficient-fields result, required equal currencies, and added mixed-currency fixtures; Contributor 09 retested and approved the fix. Approval retained concern that the original 45-day reference-free reversal window might be too permissive until labelled data existed.

When a reviewer found 11 technically correct but individually unhelpful flags from one correction batch, Contributor 01 proposed and implemented accessible expandable grouping by contract, posting date and reason while preserving every underlying flag; Contributor 01 later fixed a keyboard-focus regression and added a keyboard test. Contributor 07 advised view-level grouping because batch identifiers were not guaranteed in the scheduled feed; the implementation suppressed no rules.

In the labelled pilot sample, four reviewers classified 63 flags as 45 useful, 12 incorrect and 6 unclear; most incorrect flags were heuristic reversal matches lacking references. These were combined reviewer labels, not an independent missed-exception audit; exact duplicates had no incorrect labels in this sample only.

Using those labels, Contributor 01 proposed a 14-day confident-reversal window and match-basis display, then responded to Contributor 06's late-adjustment concern with three states: up to 14 days confident, 15–45 days visible as possible late reversals, and beyond 45 days unmatched. Contributor 10—not Contributor 01—performed the production implementation and resolved integration conflicts, using Contributor 01's design and tests; Contributor 01 reviewed the final change.

A timed comparison across 24 statements already suspected to contain exceptions, spanning the two pilot imprints and four reviewers, recorded a current-process median of 19 minutes and a Lanternleaf-assisted median of 12 minutes. The selected statements were not representative of general workload, so this bounded comparison does not establish a population-wide causal effect.

After Contributor 04 authorized continuation through April, Contributor 01 authored the monitoring and rollback runbook and delivered a 35-minute staged walkthrough to both shift leads covering grouped flags, match basis and spreadsheet fallback. The tool remained advisory, wider-imprint rollout was not approved, and ordinary reviewers were not trained in that session.

On 3 April, an export type change caused a silent zero-row load and about a two-hour delay; Contributor 01 acknowledged missing type validation, then implemented fail-closed checks, visible received-versus-expected types and a regression fixture. The cause was shared: Contributor 07 owned the unannounced export change, while Contributor 01 owned the validation omission; the runbook's spreadsheet fallback limited the delay.

The April run resumed after the schema fix with no further load failures, and reviewers said grouping made the correction batch manageable. The spreadsheet remained open for the first hour and one lead still exported rows for annotations; the close recommendation was limited continuation, not general rollout.

In May, across the same two imprints, Lanternleaf was available for 41 statements: 34 were reviewed primarily in the queue and 7 primarily in spreadsheets; the recorded median review time was 13 minutes. Eight statements lacked usable timing entries and no missed-exception audit was conducted.

By June, both shift leads still used Lanternleaf and 2 of 6 ordinary reviewers opened the queue themselves; the other four received exports or stayed in spreadsheets. This was continuing local use, not rollout to other imprints.

Afterwards, Finance deferred adding reversal references to the scheduled feed until its autumn planning round, leaving false-alert performance dependent on heuristic matching and no owner or date for broader rollout. The pilot could continue with confidence states, but that did not resolve the external feed dependency.

By July, bulk notes for grouped flags remained in the backlog, so annotations still lived in spreadsheet exports. The issue was classified as an inconvenience rather than a processing blocker.
